To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ambulatory blood pressure (BP) monitoring is superior to office BP measurement for predicting future hypertension and that ambulatory BP tracking coefficients are higher than those for office BP, especially for diastolic blood pressure and pulse pressure.

24-h ambulatory BP tracking is more stable than office BP, that daytime BP tracks better than nighttime BP, that BP variability and dipping track poorly, and that males have higher BP tracking stability than females.

office BP and ambulatory BP had moderate-to-relative high tracking coefficients from childhood to early adult hood, and males had significantly higher tracking stabilities for office SBP and DBP, and ambulatory PP compared to females.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability of BP tracking from childhood to adulthood, and its dependence on FH, ethnicity and gender.
the tracking stability of ABP, BPV and dipping in a large cohort of adolescents, and the influence of ethnicity, gender and FH on the tracking coefficients.
the stability of office BP, ambulatory BP and BPV from childhood to early adult age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tracking coefficients of BP, BPV and dipping are low to moderate and are not significantly different between European Americans and African Americans.
the tracking coefficients for office BP and ABP are moderate-to-relatively good, but the tracking coefficients for BPV and dipping measures are low.
the tracking stability of BP and BPV is higher in males than in females and higher in subjects with a positive FH than those with a FH negative for EH.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the stability of BP tracking from childhood to adulthood is moderate-to-high for office BP and ambulatory BP, moderate-to-low for BPV and dipping, and that males, African Americans, and those with a positive FH have higher tracking stability than females, European Americans and those with a negative EH FH.
ABP tracking is superior to office BP tracking, and that ABP tracking of SBP and DBP are equally good, whereas PP tracking is better for ambulatory BP than office BP.

the tracking stability of BP and its components in childhood and young adulthood is similar in African Americans and European Americans, and that males have better tracking stability than females, but only for office and ambulatory BP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tracking of BP, BPV and dipping is not as stable as previously reported.
ABP is a better predictor of future BP levels than office BP.
BPV and dipping measures are not good candidates to predict adult BP.
